title: Polynomial identity testing: randomized polynomial vs deterministic (open)
problem_statement: Given an arithmetic circuit C computing a polynomial over a field F (or the integers), decide whether the polynomial is identically zero.

input.parameter: s = circuit size (number of gates); the degree d <= 2^s.
input.size_measure: O(s log s) bits plus constants.

algorithms.name: expand into monomials
algorithms.idea: Symbolically expand the circuit into a sum of monomials and check that all coefficients vanish.
algorithms.time_complexity: exponential in s in general (a size-s circuit can have 2^Omega(s) monomials, e.g. prod_i (x_i + 1))

algorithms.name: Schwartz-Zippel random evaluation
algorithms.idea: Evaluate C at a random point from S^n for a finite set S; a nonzero polynomial of degree d vanishes there with probability <= d/|S|.
algorithms.pseudocode: pick r uniformly from S^n with |S| >= 2d; accept 'zero' iff C(r) = 0 (repeat to reduce error)
algorithms.time_complexity: poly(s) (over Z, evaluate modulo a random prime to keep numbers small)

relationship: Randomized polynomial time (coRP) is known; a deterministic polynomial algorithm is OPEN. Kabanets and Impagliazzo showed that derandomizing PIT would imply circuit lower bounds that are themselves long-standing open problems.

sources.authors: DeMillo, R. A.; Lipton, R. J.
sources.title: A probabilistic remark on algebraic program testing
Fast probabilistic algorithms for verification of polynomial identities
Derandomizing polynomial identity tests means proving circuit lower bounds

caveats: Deterministic polynomial-time PIT is known for many restricted circuit classes (e.g. read-once formulas, bounded-depth special cases). AKS primality is a derandomization of one specific identity test, (X + a)^N = X^N + a.
notes: The canonical example where randomness is known to help and nobody can remove it. Compare primality-miller-rabin-vs-aks, where the derandomization succeeded.
